name: Robert Manewitz
bio: Robert Manewitz was one of five St. Louis Smith Act defendants convicted in 1956 of conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government. After the Supreme Court's Yates decision their convictions were reversed and a retrial ordered; in October 1958 the government 'reluctantly' dropped further prosecution.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: Marcus Murphy
bio: Marcus Murphy was one of the five St. Louis Smith Act defendants convicted in 1956 of conspiring to advocate revolution. Their convictions were set aside under the Yates standard and a new trial ordered; the government abandoned the case in October 1958.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: James E. Forest
bio: James E. Forest was one of the five St. Louis Smith Act defendants — tried with his wife Dorothy Forest and William Sentner — convicted in 1956 and then freed when the Court of Appeals reversed the convictions under the Yates decision and the government dropped the retrial in October 1958.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: Billy Allen
bio: Billy Allen was one of six Detroit Smith Act defendants whose convictions were set aside after the Yates decision. Through 1958 they awaited the government's decision on whether to retry them; the prosecutions were ultimately abandoned.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Convicted; new trial ordered after Yates

name: Joseph Russo
bio: Joseph Russo of Boston was indicted under the membership clause of the Smith Act — which made knowing membership in the Communist Party a crime — and was awaiting trial in 1958 as that clause was tested in the Scales and Lightfoot cases.
charges: Smith Act — knowing membership in the Communist Party

name: Paul Bowen
bio: Paul Bowen was a Seattle Smith Act defendant, one of those tried in the Northwest prosecutions for conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government. He was acquitted, and afterward spoke publicly about the case.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: Herbert Phillips
bio: Herbert J. Phillips was a former University of Washington philosophy professor — one of the first scholars fired in the postwar loyalty purges. As a witness in the Seattle Smith Act trial he refused to name colleagues in the Communist Party and was cited for contempt, facing three years; the Ninth Circuit reversed the citation in 1958, putting him 'out of jeopardy.'
charges: Contempt — refusing to name Communist Party colleagues at the Seattle Smith Act trial
convicted: Cited for contempt; reversed by the Ninth Circuit (1958)
sentence: Faced three years for contempt; citation reversed

name: Fred M. Fine
bio: Fred M. Fine was one of six Communist Party leaders convicted in the second New York Smith Act trial (1956). In August 1958 the U.S. Court of Appeals reversed their convictions and dismissed the indictment, holding the evidence showed only 'teaching and advocacy,' not incitement to action.
charges: Smith Act — teaching and advocating the overthrow of the government
convicted: Convicted 1956; reversed and indictment dismissed August 1958

name: Al Fisher
bio: Al Fisher was a West Coast woodworkers' union official arrested in 1954 on his way to picket duty during a strike and charged with falsely signing the non-Communist affidavit required of union officers under the Taft-Hartley Act. Subjected to two trials and two appeals and facing five years, he sought review in the Supreme Court.
charges: Taft-Hartley Act — falsely signing a non-Communist affidavit
sentence: Faced up to 5 years; seeking Supreme Court review

name: William Mackie
bio: William Mackie was a 49-year-old Portland, Oregon house painter who fought deportation from 1948 onward over alleged Communist Party membership in 1937–39. In 1958 Federal Judge Gus Solomon called the case 'outrageous' but refused to dismiss the deportation order; Mackie refused to identify associates.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — alleged past Communist Party membership

name: Lena Davis Scherer
bio: Lena Davis Scherer, who came from Russia in 1913 and was the wife of labor organizer Marcel Scherer, was arrested for deportation in 1958 on a charge of being a present member of the Communist Party. She was freed on $2,500 bail while the government disputed her claim of derivative citizenship.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — alleged present Communist Party membership
convicted: Arrested for deportation; free on bail

name: Gus Polites
bio: Gus Polites was a 59-year-old Detroit restaurant and auto worker who had come from Greece in 1916. In 1958 he was fighting deportation on grounds that included his participation in unemployed demonstrations in the 1930s and his union organizing.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — 1930s unemployed demonstrations and union activity

name: August Wilhelm Lahtinen
bio: August Wilhelm Lahtinen was a Finnish-born New York newspaperman, in the United States since 1914, against whom deportation proceedings were begun in 1958 on the sole ground that he had belonged to the Finnish Workers Federation — a leftist organization defunct since 1944 — treated by the government as Communist affiliation.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — membership in the Finnish Workers Federation

name: John Janosco
bio: John Janosco was a western field representative of the United Packinghouse Workers in Los Angeles whom the Justice Department tried to deport for alleged affiliation with the Socialist Workers Party in 1937–40. In March 1958 a hearing officer ruled the government had failed to substantiate the charges, and he won.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — alleged Socialist Workers Party affiliation

name: Benjamin Cruz
bio: Benjamin Cruz was a Guatemalan-born officer of the Furniture Workers Union in Los Angeles who in 1958 was served with notice of denaturalization proceedings for allegedly denying Communist Party membership in his 1945 citizenship application.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act denaturalization — alleged concealment of Communist Party membership
sentence: Facing loss of citizenship; fighting denaturalization

name: Louis Zuker
bio: Dr. Louis Zuker was a 63-year-old Cleveland optometrist who had come from Poland some fifty years earlier. In 1958 he won his appeal from a deportation order based on alleged Communist Party membership, the Board of Immigration Appeals having found the government's witnesses unreliable.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — alleged Communist Party membership
sentence: Deportation order set aside on appeal

name: Edo Mita
bio: Edo Mita was a Japanese-American in Los Angeles whose deportation case, grounded in alleged Communist political association, was ordered reheard in 1958 under the Supreme Court's Rowoldt decision, which had held that nominal past Communist membership was not a basis for deportation.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — alleged Communist association
convicted: Deportation case reheard under the Rowoldt decision

name: Morris Rubin
bio: Morris Rubin was a skilled upholsterer and a charter member of the Furniture Workers Union in Los Angeles who lived for seven years under a deportation order issued under the Walter-McCarran Act. He died on Nov. 6, 1958, a day after immigration agents visited his home.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation
sentence: Died Nov. 6, 1958 while under deportation order

name: Paul Novick
bio: Paul Novick was the editor of the Yiddish-language daily Morning Freiheit in New York, one of dozens of foreign-born Americans facing denaturalization in 1958 on charges of having failed to disclose Communist Party membership when they became citizens.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act denaturalization — alleged undisclosed Communist Party membership

name: Charles Collins
bio: Charles Collins, once head of the New York Hotel Trades Union, was among the foreign-born Americans facing denaturalization in 1958 on charges of having concealed Communist Party membership in their citizenship applications — proceedings stalled by the Supreme Court's Nowak and Maisenberg rulings.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act denaturalization — alleged undisclosed Communist Party membership
